content:
Facing a surge in "AI slop" bug reports, Apple has recently adjusted its bug bounty program. Details below.

Apple Limits Unprocessed Vulnerability Submissions

Apple confirmed to the Financial Times that it has "set submission caps and a 30-day cooling-off period for its internal vulnerability portal, requiring users to apply for higher quotas."

These measures, implemented in June, aim to address an industry-wide surge in vulnerability reports. As large language models grow ever more powerful—capable of finding, chaining, and exploiting vulnerabilities—review teams struggle to cope with the flood of submissions.

A few weeks ago, Apple already confirmed that, in response to these AI tools, it was accelerating the pace of security updates, releasing ahead of schedule patches originally slated for last week's 26.6 release, shipping iOS 26.5.2 and other system fixes.

Across all of these systems' security notes, Apple thanked researchers using AI tools from companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Z.ai for helping discover multiple vulnerabilities.

One of the teams credited was Calif.io, which said in May that, using Anthropic's Mythos Preview model, it built a working macOS kernel memory-corruption exploit on the M5 chip in just five days.

Days before the Financial Times story published, GitHub introduced tiering to its own bug bounty program, aimed at curbing AI slop while distinguishing submissions from seasoned security researchers.

The FT report tells the story of Bynario—a seven-person cybersecurity startup that has used AI tools and models to find bugs in recent years, submitting five reports to Apple this year and eight last year, "one of which was patched in a November software update," only to be rejected.

After the FT report ran, Apple has since reached out to Bynario and is reviewing its findings, including a privilege-escalation exploit chain that could give attackers full control of a Mac.

Apple's statement to the Financial Times on the recent bug bounty program changes:

The company added that researchers "can easily apply for higher limits at any time to ensure important reports reach our security team."
